summary: RFC 8141 changed how formal URN namespaces are registered, dropping the old requirement for IETF Consensus. This document handles the transition, so that registrations and rules that depended on the old procedure are updated to fit the new model.

eli5.summary: The old sign-up rules for a type of name were too strict, so they were relaxed. This explains how to move over to the easier rules.

questions: how are urn namespaces registered now
what is a formal urn namespace
what happened to rfc 3044 and rfc 3187
subtitle: Moves the ISBN and ISSN URN namespaces to the relaxed registration rules of RFC 8141 and retires their old RFCs.

tldr.problem: The original URN namespace registration procedure required IETF Consensus, which discouraged registrations and invited names being used without any registration at all.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8141 changed the model, and this document records how selected existing registrations (ISBN and ISSN) were moved to it, what happens to NBN, and how IANA should treat all other older registrations.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3044 (ISSN) and RFC 3187 (ISBN) are obsoleted and moved to Historic; their descriptions now live in registration templates in the IANA registry.

today: RFC 8254 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 3044 and RFC 3187, which are now Historic, and the ISBN and ISSN namespaces are defined by templates in the IANA URN Namespaces registry under RFC 8141.

sections.title: Why a Transition Was Needed
sections.content:
In the late 1990s the IETF URN Working Group wanted to show that URN syntax could carry existing identifier systems. RFC 2288 showed that ISBN, ISSN and SICI could be used as URNs, but it did not formally register namespaces. Later, namespaces were registered for ISBN (RFC 3187), ISSN (RFC 3044) and NBN (RFC 3188), among many others.

This document does four things: it describes the instructions developed with IANA to adapt selected registrations to the new model, obsoletes the separate ISSN and ISBN RFCs, gives the status of NBNs under the new definitions, and offers IANA suggestions for all other existing registrations.
sections.eli5: Long ago, people showed that book and magazine numbers could be turned into special names. Now the sign-up rules changed, so this note tidies up the old paperwork.

sections.title: The Problem With IETF Consensus
sections.content:
The predecessor procedure, RFC 3406, required IETF Consensus for formal namespaces. According to this document, that requirement discouraged some registrations and increased the risk of problems, including use of names without registration ("squatting").

Unregistered use is risky because the same name could end up identifying different namespaces with different rules, causing considerable confusion. RFC 8141 therefore adopted a model that encourages registration of every namespace that follows the formal namespace syntax, collecting as much information as is consistent with that goal.
sections.eli5: If getting a name approved is a huge hassle, people just use the name anyway. Then two people might use the same name for different things. Making sign-up easier avoids that mix-up.

sections.title: ISBN and ISSN Move to New Templates
sections.content:
RFC 3044 (ISSN) and RFC 3187 (ISBN) were identified as Historic at the same time this document was published. New registration templates for both namespaces were already submitted and incorporated into the IANA URN Namespaces registry. The templates reflect the new format and also substantive changes to the namespace definitions. Approving them made the older templates obsolete.

The ISBN namespace now follows ISO 2108:2017. It allows both the old ten-character numbers described in RFC 3187 (formerly ISBN-10) and the thirteen-character identifiers introduced in ISO 2108:2005 (formerly ISBN-13).

The ISSN namespace now follows ISO 3297:2007, which introduced the linking ISSN (ISSN-L). An ISSN-L is designated for all media of a serial publication, however many there are, whereas a traditional ISSN applies to a single medium only, such as the printed version.

For both namespaces, registration practice is expected to evolve with the ISO standards without resubmitting the templates or going through formal IETF or IANA update approval.
sections.eli5: Two old rulebooks, one for book numbers and one for magazine numbers, were put on the shelf as history. Up-to-date forms now say how those numbers become names, and they can keep up with changes by themselves.

sections.title: National Bibliography Numbers
sections.content:
An NBN is not a formal international standard or even a single identifier system. It is an umbrella for the identifiers that national libraries and their partners use for resources that have no other identifier. For example, a book received by legal deposit without an ISBN gets a local identifier from the national library, which the NBN specification turns into a globally unique URN such as urn:nbn:fi-fe19981001.

RFC 3188 holds both the namespace registration and generic information about NBNs, including their syntax. That syntax guarantees uniqueness by requiring country codes and institutional identifiers as part of the Namespace Specific String. This document does not obsolete RFC 3188; it says that when RFC 3188 is revised, the revision should come with a template that revises the URN:NBN registration.
sections.eli5: When a library gets a book with no number, it gives the book its own label. The NBN rules turn that label into a name that is different from every other library's labels.

sections.title: Every Other Existing Registration
sections.content:
Many other URN namespaces are registered in the RFC Series and the IANA registry. This document says that, in general, those registrations are still appropriate but omit some information called for in RFC 8141. Reregistration with new templates is recommended but not required.

Until a registration is updated as RFC 8141 provides, its existing template should be read as neither requiring nor allowing any feature that was not allowed and specified by the earlier URN syntax (RFC 2141) and registration (RFC 3406) specifications.
sections.eli5: Old sign-ups stay valid. They just keep following the old rules until their owners choose to fill in the new form.

sections.title: What IANA Does
sections.content:
IANA completed the updates for the URN ISSN and ISBN registry entries so they reflect the new templates that comply with RFC 8141. For other namespaces, templates that conform to the newer rules may be substituted when they are available. Neither this document nor RFC 8141 supersedes any existing registration other than ISBN and ISSN, so IANA must be prepared to maintain a registry mixing old-style and new-style templates.

The portions of the ISBN and ISSN registrations that point to ISO standards are meant to identify the current versions, which may change, not only the versions active when this document was approved. That relies on ISO TC 46 and its registration authorities to keep URN references stable.
sections.eli5: The librarian of the registry updated two entries and now keeps a shelf with some old forms and some new ones side by side.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Particular URN namespaces and their registrations might conceivably have security implications, but this specification only transitions a set of registrations and does not have such implications. Security issues of individual namespaces are expected to be listed in their registration templates, as RFC 8141 specifies.
sections.eli5: This note only moves paperwork around, so it adds no new danger. Each kind of name is expected to list its own safety notes on its form.
